name: simple_reflex_agent
definition: Reacts to current percept using condition-action rules with no memory of past states. The simplest agent architecture defined in classical AI literature.
how_it_works: Receives a percept from the environment; looks up a matching condition in a fixed set of if-then rules; executes the mapped action immediately. No internal state is maintained between cycles.
strengths: Extremely fast response with minimal compute; easy to implement, test and reason about; deterministic and auditable behaviour.
limitations: Cannot handle partially observable environments; ignores history so it loops in the same state; brittle when rules do not cover a situation.
typical_examples: Thermostat controllers, spam filters with keyword rules, simple IRC bots, early video-game NPCs.

name: model_based_reflex_agent
definition: Maintains an internal model of the world to handle partial observability while still using condition-action rules for decisions.
how_it_works: Updates an internal world-state representation each cycle by combining the current percept with the previous state and a transition model. Condition-action rules are then applied to this enriched state rather than the raw percept alone.
strengths: Handles partial observability; avoids repeating actions that have already changed hidden state; still fast enough for real-time use.
limitations: World model must be hand-crafted or learned and can go stale; complexity grows with environment size; still cannot pursue goals beyond the fixed rule set.
typical_examples: Autonomous vacuum robots maintaining a map of cleaned cells, early autonomous vehicle lane-keeping systems, rule-based fraud detection with rolling window state.

name: goal_based_agent
definition: Has explicit goals and searches for action sequences that lead to goal states, enabling planning beyond the immediate next action.
how_it_works: Represents the current state, one or more goal states, and a set of possible actions. Uses search algorithms (BFS, A*, MCTS) to find a sequence of actions that transforms the current state into a goal state before executing.
strengths: Can solve complex multi-step problems; goals are explicit and interpretable; flexible since changing the goal re-plans without code changes.
limitations: Planning can be computationally expensive; requires an accurate model of action effects; may fail in highly dynamic environments where the plan becomes invalid mid-execution.
typical_examples: Route-planning navigation agents, chess-playing agents, robotic assembly planners, task scheduling assistants.

name: utility_based_agent
definition: Assigns a utility (preference) score to states and selects actions that maximise expected utility across possible future states.
how_it_works: Extends goal-based agents by replacing binary goal satisfaction with a continuous utility function. Evaluates each candidate action by its expected utility—accounting for uncertainty—and selects the action with the highest value.
strengths: Makes rational trade-offs among competing objectives; handles uncertainty and risk naturally; produces nuanced behaviour beyond simple pass/fail goals.
limitations: Designing a good utility function is hard and often encodes hidden assumptions; computationally expensive for large state spaces; utility maximisation can produce unintended instrumental behaviours.
typical_examples: Recommendation system agents optimising engagement vs. diversity, trading bots maximising risk-adjusted return, resource allocation agents in cloud scheduling.

name: learning_agent
definition: Has a learning element that improves performance from experience using feedback signals, gradually refining its behaviour policy over time.
how_it_works: Contains four components: performance element (acts), critic (evaluates actions against a standard), learning element (improves performance element using critic feedback), and problem generator (proposes exploratory actions). Feedback drives policy updates via RL, supervised fine-tuning or other learning algorithms.
strengths: Improves automatically over time; can adapt to environments too complex to hand-code; generalises from examples to novel situations.
limitations: Requires significant data and compute to train; learning can be unstable; may exploit reward functions in unintended ways; requires careful design of feedback signals.
typical_examples: RLHF-trained LLM assistants, reinforcement learning game agents (AlphaGo, OpenAI Five), self-improving code-generation agents.

name: conversational_agent
definition: Engages in multi-turn natural language conversation with users to answer questions, provide information, or assist with tasks through dialogue.
how_it_works: Maintains a conversation history (messages list), passes it with each turn to an LLM, and returns the model's reply. May be augmented with retrieval, tools and memory to ground responses and extend capabilities.
strengths: Natural user interface; broad applicability; easy to deploy via chat platforms; can combine knowledge from pre-training with real-time retrieval.
limitations: May hallucinate facts; conversation context window limits length; difficult to maintain consistent persona across very long sessions; latency can degrade experience.
typical_examples: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini chat, customer support bots, HR FAQ assistants, health symptom checkers.

name: workflow_agent
definition: Automates a defined sequence of steps in a business or technical process by integrating with multiple tools and APIs in a structured pipeline.
how_it_works: Receives a trigger (schedule, event or user request); executes a predefined or dynamically planned sequence of tool calls, data transformations and conditional branches; produces a structured output or side-effect such as a sent email or updated record.
strengths: Reliable, auditable automation; integrates heterogeneous systems; reduces manual effort; deterministic when the workflow is fixed.
limitations: Rigid to scope changes without workflow redesign; debugging cross-system failures is complex; may require significant integration work upfront.
typical_examples: Invoice processing pipelines, CI/CD orchestration agents, data ETL agents, HR onboarding automation.

name: voice_agent
definition: Receives spoken input via speech-to-text (STT), processes it with an LLM or dialogue manager, and responds with spoken output via text-to-speech (TTS).
how_it_works: Audio is captured and streamed to an STT engine which produces a transcript. The transcript is processed by an LLM-based dialogue manager (with optional tool calls). The response text is passed to a TTS engine and played back. Turn-taking logic handles interruptions and silence detection.
strengths: Hands-free interaction; accessible to non-typing users; natural for real-time customer service and IVR replacements.
limitations: STT errors propagate; latency compounds across STT+LLM+TTS pipeline; difficult to handle ambiguous or accented speech; privacy concerns with always-on microphones.
typical_examples: Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant, voice IVR systems, voice-controlled IoT devices, call-centre voice bots.

name: knowledge_rag_agent
definition: Answers questions by retrieving relevant documents from a knowledge base and grounding responses in retrieved content using the Retrieval-Augmented Generation pattern.
how_it_works: Embeds the user query and searches a vector store or keyword index for the most relevant document chunks. Retrieved passages are injected into the LLM prompt as context. The LLM synthesises an answer grounded in the evidence, reducing hallucination risk.
strengths: Keeps responses factual and up-to-date without full fine-tuning; supports citations; knowledge base can be updated independently of the model.
limitations: Retrieval quality limits answer quality; chunking strategy significantly affects results; latency from retrieval adds to response time; long documents may exceed context.
typical_examples: Enterprise Q&A bots over internal wikis, legal document assistants, medical literature search agents, customer support agents over product docs.

name: vision_multimodal_agent
definition: Processes and reasons over images, video or other non-text modalities alongside text to accomplish tasks requiring cross-modal understanding.
how_it_works: Accepts inputs in multiple modalities (image, audio, video, text). A multimodal encoder (vision transformer, audio encoder) converts each modality to tokens in a shared embedding space. The LLM backbone reasons over all tokens jointly to produce a text or structured output.
strengths: Solves tasks impossible for text-only models; can inspect charts, diagrams and scenes; enables visual QA, document parsing, and image-based code generation.
limitations: Multimodal models are larger and slower; image inputs consume many tokens; hallucinations can occur on fine visual details; video processing is expensive.
typical_examples: GPT-4V image analysis, Gemini multimodal reasoning, visual document parsing, medical image analysis assistants.

name: research_agent
definition: Autonomously searches the web and databases, synthesises information from multiple sources, and produces structured research reports with citations.
how_it_works: Receives a research topic or question; decomposes it into sub-queries; uses web search, academic database and tool APIs to retrieve sources; reads and extracts key facts; synthesises findings into a coherent report with citations; iterates if gaps remain.
strengths: Covers vast information spaces quickly; produces cited, structured output; reduces research time dramatically; can re-run to update findings.
limitations: May surface low-quality or biased sources; fact-checking is imperfect; cannot access paywalled content; synthesis quality depends heavily on retrieval quality.
typical_examples: Perplexity deep research, OpenAI deep research mode, Gemini deep research, custom academic literature review agents.

name: coding_agent
definition: Generates, reviews, debugs and executes code to solve software engineering tasks, interacting with IDEs, terminals and code repositories.
how_it_works: Receives a software task description; generates code using an LLM; executes it in a sandboxed environment; analyses the output or error; iterates by editing and re-running until tests pass or the task is complete. Can interact with git, linters and package managers.
strengths: Dramatically accelerates software development; can iterate autonomously; handles boilerplate; integrates with existing toolchains.
limitations: May generate plausible but incorrect code; sandbox escapes are a security risk; lacks understanding of large-codebase architecture without context; can introduce subtle bugs.
typical_examples: GitHub Copilot Workspace, Devin, Claude Code, Cursor Agent, OpenAI Codex agent.

name: browser_computer_use_agent
definition: Controls a web browser or full desktop to interact with websites and GUI applications as a human would, using visual understanding and UI automation.
how_it_works: Takes a goal; opens a browser or desktop session; uses vision models or accessibility trees to understand the current UI state; generates mouse, keyboard or touch actions; executes them via browser automation APIs (Playwright, Puppeteer) or OS-level injection; observes the result and continues until the goal is achieved.
strengths: Can automate any web or desktop workflow without an API; works with legacy software; handles dynamic UIs.
limitations: Fragile to UI changes; slow compared to API calls; difficult to handle CAPTCHAs and authentication flows; high error rate on complex multi-step tasks; raises security concerns.
typical_examples: Anthropic Computer Use, OpenAI Operator, browser-use library agents, RPA bots augmented with LLMs.

name: personal_assistant_agent
definition: Manages a user's tasks, calendar, email and information needs as a persistent, personalised helper with memory across sessions.
how_it_works: Maintains a user model and personal memory store. On each interaction, retrieves relevant context (past preferences, ongoing tasks, calendar state) and uses tools (email APIs, calendar APIs, task managers, search) to fulfil requests. Writes outcomes back to memory for future reference.
strengths: Personalised over time; proactively surfaces relevant information; reduces cognitive load; integrates disparate personal information.
limitations: Requires broad API access raising privacy concerns; mistakes in autonomous actions (sent emails, deleted events) are hard to reverse; trust calibration is difficult.
typical_examples: Apple Intelligence, Microsoft 365 Copilot personal assistant, Notion AI assistant, custom AI executive assistant bots.

name: data_analysis_agent
definition: Writes and executes code or SQL to analyse datasets, generate visualisations and produce insights on demand from natural language questions.
how_it_works: Receives a data question or task; connects to datasets via file access or database connectors; generates pandas, SQL or R code to perform analysis; executes in a sandboxed interpreter; returns results, tables and charts; iterates if the output does not answer the question.
strengths: Democratises data analysis; reproducible; can handle datasets too large to fit in a prompt; produces visual outputs.
limitations: Requires access to data which may be sensitive; generated SQL or code can be incorrect; visualisation quality varies; hallucinations about numerical results are dangerous.
typical_examples: Code Interpreter in ChatGPT, Gemini Advanced data analysis, Julius AI, enterprise BI agents on warehouse data.

name: commerce_transaction_agent
definition: Executes purchases, negotiations or financial transactions autonomously on behalf of a user, with configurable authorisation controls and spending limits.
how_it_works: Receives a commercial intent (buy, negotiate, refund); verifies the action against a user-defined policy (spending limit, allowed merchants); interacts with payment APIs, e-commerce platforms or negotiation counterparties; confirms execution and reports back; logs all transactions for audit.
strengths: Automates tedious purchasing workflows; can optimise for price or speed; enforces spending policies automatically.
limitations: Irreversible financial actions require extremely high reliability; fraud and social engineering risk; regulatory compliance complexity; trust and liability concerns.
typical_examples: Amazon agent purchasing, travel booking agents, automated procurement bots, forex execution agents.

name: security_monitoring_agent
definition: Continuously monitors systems, logs and network traffic for anomalies and threats, escalating or responding automatically to detected incidents.
how_it_works: Ingests streams of security telemetry (logs, metrics, alerts); applies anomaly detection, signature matching and LLM-based reasoning to triage alerts; correlates events across sources; determines severity; either automatically remediates low-risk events or escalates high-risk ones to human analysts with a detailed report.
strengths: Continuous coverage; faster triage than human analysts; correlates signals across large data volumes; reduces alert fatigue with intelligent prioritisation.
limitations: High false-positive rates can erode trust; autonomous remediation carries risk of service disruption; adversaries can probe agent behaviour to evade detection; requires access to sensitive systems.
typical_examples: Darktrace AI analyst, Microsoft Sentinel AI, custom SOC agents on SIEM data, cloud security posture agents.

name: vertical_industry_agent
definition: A specialised agent fine-tuned or configured for a specific industry with domain-specific tools, knowledge bases and compliance constraints.
how_it_works: Built by combining a foundation model with domain-specific fine-tuning or RAG over industry corpora (medical literature, legal case law, financial regulations); equipped with industry-specific tool integrations (EHR systems, legal databases, trading platforms); governed by compliance rules baked into guardrails.
strengths: Deep domain expertise; meets industry-specific regulatory requirements; more accurate than a general assistant in its domain; reduces need for expert consultants.
limitations: Expensive to build and maintain; regulatory approval may be required; fine-tuning can degrade general reasoning; domain knowledge goes stale.
typical_examples: Nabla healthcare assistant, Harvey legal AI, BloombergGPT financial assistant, industrial maintenance agents.

name: simulation_game_agent
definition: Operates within simulated or game environments, making decisions to achieve in-simulation goals, used for research, synthetic data generation and game NPC behaviour.
how_it_works: Receives observations from a game or simulation engine (state vectors, pixel frames); processes them through a policy network or LLM-based planner; outputs actions in the action space of the environment; collects rewards and optionally updates its policy; operates in a closed loop with the simulator.
strengths: Safe environment to test agent capabilities; generates training data at scale; enables study of multi-agent dynamics; no real-world risk.
limitations: Sim-to-real gap means capabilities may not transfer; requires simulator infrastructure; compute-intensive for large simulations; game-specific skills rarely generalise.
typical_examples: AlphaStar (StarCraft), OpenAI Five (Dota), Voyager (Minecraft), generative agents in social simulation.

name: long_horizon_agent
definition: Executes tasks requiring many sequential steps over extended time periods, maintaining state and context across dozens to hundreds of actions.
how_it_works: Decomposes a high-level goal into a plan; executes steps iteratively using tools and memory; persists intermediate state to durable storage so work survives interruptions; monitors progress against the original plan and replans when blocked; requests human assistance only when genuinely stuck.
strengths: Handles complex multi-stage projects autonomously; reduces need for constant human supervision; can run overnight or over days.
limitations: Reliability degrades with horizon length as errors compound; long context management is challenging; difficult to test end-to-end; catastrophic failure modes when unrecoverable errors occur.
typical_examples: Devin software engineering agent, AutoGPT-style agents, overnight data pipeline agents, autonomous scientific experiment agents.

name: hierarchical_agent
definition: Structured as a tree of agents: a supervisor breaks goals into subtasks, delegates to specialists, aggregates results, and maintains quality oversight.
how_it_works: A top-level orchestrator receives the goal and produces a decomposed plan. Each subtask is dispatched to a specialist worker agent. Workers execute and return results. The orchestrator evaluates results, handles failures by re-delegating, and assembles the final output.
strengths: Scales to complex tasks; specialist agents can be tuned for their domain; isolates failures to subtask level; natural fit for parallel execution.
limitations: Communication overhead grows with depth; orchestrator is a single point of failure; requires careful interface design between layers; debugging cross-layer failures is complex.
typical_examples: LangGraph supervisor graphs, AutoGen group chat with manager, CrewAI hierarchical crews, enterprise agent pipelines.

name: multi_agent_system
definition: Two or more agents interacting, collaborating or competing to solve problems beyond any single agent's capability.
how_it_works: Multiple agents, each with its own context, tools and potentially different models, communicate through a shared message bus, blackboard or direct messaging protocol. They may have symmetric roles (peers) or asymmetric roles (supervisor/worker). Coordination mechanisms prevent conflicts and deadlocks.
strengths: Parallel processing; specialisation; redundancy via multiple independent solvers; emergent problem-solving through agent interaction.
limitations: Coordination complexity; communication overhead; risk of conflicting actions; difficult to debug and observe; emergent behaviours can be unexpected.
typical_examples: AutoGen multi-agent conversations, Microsoft Semantic Kernel agent groups, A2A protocol-connected agent networks.

name: supervisor_orchestrator
definition: The top-level agent in a hierarchy that plans, delegates to workers, monitors quality and manages the overall workflow end-to-end.
how_it_works: Receives the user goal; produces a structured work plan; dispatches subtasks to appropriate worker agents; collects results; evaluates quality (possibly using an evaluator agent); retries or reassigns failed steps; assembles the final deliverable and reports to the user.
strengths: Centralises coordination; enables parallelism; natural audit trail through the orchestrator; can enforce global constraints and policies.
limitations: Orchestrator context window grows with task size; orchestrator failure blocks the entire pipeline; requires the orchestrator to have full visibility of the problem domain.
typical_examples: LangGraph supervisor node, AutoGen UserProxy manager, CrewAI process manager, A2A orchestrator agent.

name: worker_specialist
definition: A focused agent that receives well-defined subtasks from an orchestrator and executes them without broad planning responsibility.
how_it_works: Receives a structured task description from an orchestrator; executes using its specialised tools and knowledge; returns a structured result; handles retries within its own scope; does not need visibility of the full goal.
strengths: Highly focused; can be optimised for a narrow task; independently testable; replaceable without affecting the orchestrator.
limitations: Dependent on the orchestrator for task framing; limited ability to self-direct when the task description is ambiguous; not useful in isolation.
typical_examples: Web search worker, code execution worker, document summariser worker, database query worker in multi-agent pipelines.

name: evaluator_critic
definition: An agent whose primary role is to judge the quality, correctness or safety of another agent's output and report a structured evaluation.
how_it_works: Receives an output from a producer agent along with the original task specification and an evaluation rubric. Applies the rubric to generate a structured critique with scores, identified issues and improvement suggestions. Sends the critique back to the orchestrator or directly to the producer.
strengths: Improves output quality through automated review; enables iterative refinement without human review of every output; can enforce style, accuracy and safety standards.
limitations: Critic quality depends on its own reasoning ability; critics can agree with errors they should catch; adds latency and cost to each generation cycle.
typical_examples: Self-refinement critics, LLM-as-judge evaluators, automated PR review agents, test-writing agents that verify code correctness.

name: planner_agent
definition: Decomposes high-level goals into structured plans (steps, dependencies, assignments) without necessarily executing them, providing a roadmap for other agents.
how_it_works: Receives a goal; analyses it to identify required steps, their dependencies and the best order of execution; identifies which tools or agent types each step requires; produces a machine-readable plan (JSON DAG, task list); hands the plan to an executor or orchestrator.
strengths: Separation of concerns enables better planning quality; plan can be reviewed by humans or validators before execution; planner can optimise task ordering for parallelism.
limitations: Planning quality degrades for tasks requiring real-time information not available at plan time; plan can become stale as execution proceeds; adds an extra LLM call before work begins.
typical_examples: GPT-4 task planner in AutoGPT, LLM-based DAG planner in LangGraph, strategic planning agents in multi-agent research systems.

name: router_agent
definition: Classifies incoming requests and directs them to the appropriate specialised agent or processing pipeline based on intent, topic or format.
how_it_works: Receives an input (user message, event, document); applies a classification model or LLM prompt to determine the intent and required handler; routes the input to the matching agent or pipeline with any necessary context; may also apply load balancing across multiple instances of the same handler.
strengths: Enables a system to handle heterogeneous inputs without monolithic logic; keeps specialist agents focused; easy to extend by adding new routes.
limitations: Misclassification sends requests to the wrong handler; routing logic must be kept in sync with available agents; adds a round-trip latency; can become a bottleneck.
typical_examples: Intent-based chatbot routers, API gateway agents, multi-domain customer service dispatchers, model selector agents.

name: tool_using_agent
definition: An agent defined by its ability to call external tools (APIs, code interpreters, databases) as part of its reasoning loop to extend its capabilities beyond text generation.
how_it_works: At each reasoning step, the agent can decide to call a tool (from a registered catalogue), provide arguments, receive the tool result, and incorporate it into its next reasoning step. This loop continues until the agent determines it has enough information to produce a final answer.
strengths: Dramatically extends LLM capability; keeps the model grounded with real data; modular since tools can be added or removed; enables real-world actions.
limitations: Tool call errors propagate into reasoning; tool descriptions must be precise; too many tools confuse the model; security risks from over-permissioned tools.
typical_examples: ReAct agents, function-calling agents using OpenAI/Anthropic/Google APIs, LangChain agent executors, MCP-connected agents.

name: memory_augmented_agent
definition: An agent with persistent external memory that it reads and writes across sessions, enabling personalisation, continuity and accumulation of knowledge over time.
how_it_works: At the start of each session, the agent queries its memory store (vector DB, key-value store or graph DB) with the current context to retrieve relevant past information. During and after the session it writes new facts, decisions and summaries back to memory. Future sessions benefit from accumulated knowledge.
strengths: Enables personalisation that improves over time; overcomes context window limits; supports long-horizon task continuity across sessions.
limitations: Memory retrieval can surface stale or incorrect information; privacy concerns with persistent user data; memory management (forgetting, updating) is complex; storage costs grow over time.
typical_examples: MemGPT/Letta agents, Zep-augmented agents, custom agents with Pinecone or Weaviate long-term memory, personal AI assistants.

name: embodied_robotic_agent
definition: An AI agent controlling a physical robot body, integrating perception of the physical world with language reasoning and motor action planning.
how_it_works: Sensor inputs (cameras, LiDAR, touch, proprioception) are processed by perception models to generate a world-state representation. An LLM or planning module reasons over the state and goal, generates a high-level action plan, which is translated into low-level motor commands by a robot controller.
strengths: Bridges language AI and physical world; can follow natural language instructions for physical tasks; enables generalisation across diverse environments.
limitations: Physical safety risk; sim-to-real gap; latency between perception and action must be low; robot hardware is expensive; reliability requirements are extremely high.
typical_examples: Google DeepMind RT-2 (robotic transformer), Figure AI humanoid with OpenAI LLM, Boston Dynamics Spot with language guidance.

name: swarm_agent
definition: One member of a swarm: a lightweight agent that works in parallel with many identical or similar agents on decomposed subtasks, with no central coordinator.
how_it_works: A task is split into independent shards. Identical or similar agents are instantiated for each shard. Each agent processes its shard independently, posts results to a shared blackboard or message bus. A merge step aggregates results. Agents may also communicate peer-to-peer to avoid duplicate work.
strengths: Massively parallel; horizontally scalable; individual agent failures do not stop the swarm; no single point of coordination failure.
limitations: Requires careful task decomposition to avoid conflicts; merge logic must handle partial failures; communication overhead grows with swarm size; emergent coordination bugs are hard to debug.
typical_examples: Particle swarm optimisation agents, parallelised web scraping agents, distributed document processing swarms, test-generation agent swarms.

name: peer_to_peer_agent
definition: An agent in a network where agents communicate directly with each other without a central orchestrator, negotiating and coordinating autonomously.
how_it_works: Agents maintain a local view of the network and discover peers via a directory or gossip protocol. They send messages directly to relevant peers using an agreed protocol (A2A, custom RPC). Coordination emerges from local rules and negotiation rather than central control. Consensus mechanisms resolve conflicts.
strengths: Highly resilient with no central point of failure; scales naturally; enables emergent cooperative behaviour; appropriate for decentralised environments.
limitations: Harder to reason about system-wide behaviour; debugging requires distributed tracing; consensus mechanisms add overhead; security is more complex without a central authority.
typical_examples: Federated learning participants, A2A peer agents, autonomous negotiation agents in supply-chain markets, distributed sensor fusion agents.

name: reactive_agent
definition: An agent that responds immediately to stimuli without deliberate planning or memory, optimised for speed and simplicity in well-defined environments.
how_it_works: Implements a direct stimulus-response mapping (rule engine, neural policy, or lookup table). On each tick, reads the current input and immediately produces an output with no internal deliberation cycle. State is entirely in the environment or the most recent observation.
strengths: Extremely low latency; simple to implement; deterministic and auditable; robust since there is no complex internal state to corrupt.
limitations: Cannot handle tasks requiring multi-step reasoning or memory; brittle outside the design envelope; cannot learn from experience without external adaptation mechanisms.
typical_examples: Real-time game bots, reflex-based robot controllers, simple IVR systems, high-frequency trading signal generators.

name: deliberative_agent
definition: An agent that explicitly plans and reasons before acting, trading speed for thoroughness and correctness in complex or novel situations.
how_it_works: Maintains an explicit world model. Before each action, runs a planning or reasoning algorithm (search, logical inference, LLM chain-of-thought) over the model to identify the best action sequence. Executes the selected action and updates the world model based on the outcome.
strengths: Produces higher-quality decisions for complex tasks; can explain its reasoning; adapts plans when outcomes differ from expectations; handles novel situations.
limitations: High latency per step; computationally expensive; planning quality depends on world model accuracy; can get stuck in loops if planning fails to converge.
typical_examples: Multi-step reasoning agents, theorem-proving agents, strategic planning agents, medical diagnosis reasoning agents.

name: hybrid_agent
definition: Combines reactive and deliberative layers: fast reflexive responses for routine situations, deliberate planning for complex or novel ones.
how_it_works: Two-layer architecture: a reactive layer handles common, well-understood stimuli with low-latency rules; a deliberative layer monitors the reactive layer, identifies situations requiring deeper reasoning, and either overrides or supplements the reactive response with a planned action.
strengths: Best of both worlds: fast for common cases, thorough for complex ones; more robust than either alone; can prioritise safety-critical reactions.
limitations: Increased architectural complexity; designing the hand-off between layers is non-trivial; potential for layer conflicts; harder to test exhaustively.
typical_examples: Autonomous vehicle systems (lane-keeping reactive + route planning deliberative), advanced game agents, enterprise chatbots with rule-based fast paths and LLM fallback.

name: autonomous_long_horizon_agent
definition: Operates for extended periods on complex multi-step tasks with minimal human intervention, managing its own planning, tool use and memory.
how_it_works: Sets its own sub-goals from a high-level objective; maintains a persistent task graph with completed, in-progress and pending nodes; executes steps using tools and code; writes intermediate results to durable storage; monitors for blockers and either works around them or escalates; resumes seamlessly after interruption.
strengths: Can complete ambitious projects autonomously over hours or days; reduces total human time investment; learns from failures within a run.
limitations: Error accumulation over long horizons; difficult to monitor and correct mid-task; risk of unrecoverable states; unpredictable resource consumption; alignment risks from unsupervised goal pursuit.
typical_examples: Devin autonomous software engineering, AutoGPT long-running tasks, AI-driven overnight research pipelines.

name: human_in_loop_agent
definition: An agent designed with explicit pause points where it solicits human review, approval or correction before proceeding with high-stakes or irreversible actions.
how_it_works: Executes autonomously until it reaches a defined checkpoint (irreversible action, low confidence, policy boundary). At the checkpoint it pauses, presents its plan or draft action to a human, and waits for approval, modification or rejection before continuing. Humans can also intervene proactively via a monitoring interface.
strengths: Prevents catastrophic autonomous errors; builds user trust; complies with regulatory requirements for human oversight; enables gradual expansion of autonomy as trust grows.
limitations: Slower than fully autonomous execution; human reviewers become a bottleneck; approval fatigue can lead to rubber-stamping; requires careful design of what triggers a checkpoint.
typical_examples: Approval-gated financial transaction agents, supervised code-deployment agents, medical AI requiring clinician sign-off, HR action agents with manager approval.

name: knowledge_base_agent
definition: Maintains and queries a structured knowledge base as its primary mode of action, using retrieval and reasoning over stored structured knowledge.
how_it_works: Connects to one or more knowledge stores (graph DB, relational DB, ontology, structured KB). Receives queries; translates them into KB query language (SPARQL, Cypher, SQL); retrieves facts; reasons over the returned structured data to produce an answer; can also update the KB with new information.
strengths: Highly accurate for queries within the KB's scope; transparent and auditable; deterministic for factual lookups; supports complex multi-hop reasoning via graph traversal.
limitations: Requires a well-maintained KB; KB coverage limits answer scope; natural language to query translation can fail; KB updates require validation to prevent corruption.
typical_examples: Enterprise knowledge graph agents, Wolfram Alpha-style computational knowledge agents, drug interaction lookup agents, ontology-grounded medical agents.

name: code_interpreter_agent
definition: An agent with a secure code execution environment as a core capability, using code as the primary medium for computation and problem-solving.
how_it_works: Integrates a sandboxed code execution kernel (Python, R, JavaScript) alongside an LLM. The agent generates code to solve sub-problems, executes it, reads the output, and uses the result to generate further code or a final answer. All execution is isolated from the host.
strengths: Exact computation via code rather than approximate LLM arithmetic; reproducible; handles data manipulation, visualisation and mathematical tasks accurately.
limitations: Sandbox escape risks if isolation is imperfect; generated code can have bugs; slow for tasks where plain text would suffice; managing library dependencies in the sandbox is non-trivial.
typical_examples: ChatGPT Code Interpreter, Gemini Advanced code execution, Jupyter AI, enterprise data analysis agents.

name: multimodal_reasoning_agent
definition: Integrates reasoning across text, images, audio and potentially video in a unified cognitive loop, treating all modalities as first-class inputs.
how_it_works: A unified multimodal model (or a composition of modality-specific encoders feeding a shared reasoning core) processes inputs from multiple modalities simultaneously. The reasoning loop can interleave modality-specific tool calls (image generation, audio synthesis) with text reasoning to produce a cross-modal output.
strengths: Solves genuinely cross-modal tasks (describe what you see and hear); enables richer interfaces; can generate multimodal outputs; strongest available modality is always leveraged.
limitations: Largest inference cost among architecture types; modality alignment errors (misattributing audio to wrong visual element); limited multimodal training data for rare modality combinations; complex prompt engineering.
typical_examples: Gemini 1.5 Pro multimodal reasoning, GPT-4o omni model, Reka multimodal agents, video understanding research agents.
